# 1. Reproduce the bug reliably first: write a minimal failing test case before changing any code, so you know exactly when it's fixed.
# 2. Read the full traceback bottom-up: the last frame shows where the error occurred, while earlier frames reveal how execution got there.

# 5. Bisect the problem: use git bisect or comment out half the code path to narrow down which change or branch introduced the failure.
# 6. Verify types at boundaries: many bugs come from str vs int, None vs empty container, or bytes vs str, so assert isinstance() at API edges.
# 7. Test boundary conditions explicitly: empty lists, index 0, index -1, off-by-one loop limits, and the last element often hide the bug.
# 8. Add temporary assertions for invariants you believe hold (e.g., assert len(data) > 0) so violations fail loudly instead of corrupting downstream state.
# 9. Explain the code aloud line by line (rubber-duck debugging); verbalizing assumptions often exposes the flawed premise before you run anything.
# 10. Strip the failing case down to a minimal reproducible example: delete unrelated code until the bug either vanishes (isolate the trigger) or persists in a tiny snippet you can reason about fully.
